The transit probability for a planet on a circular orbit is approximately \(P_{\text{transit}} \approx R_* / a\), where \(R_*\) is the stellar radius and \(a\) is the orbital semi-major axis. Since both host stars have the same radius, the ratio of transit probabilities depends only on the ratio of semi-major axes: \(\text{Prob}_1 / \text{Prob}_2 = a_2 / a_1\).

From Kepler's third law, \(a^3 \propto P^2 M_*\). Given \(P_1 = P_2 / 3\) and \(M_{*1} = 2 M_{*2}\):
\[
a_1 \propto (P_1^2 M_{*1})^{1/3} = \left( \left(\frac{P_2}{3}\right)^2 (2 M_{*2}) \right)^{1/3} = \left( \frac{2}{9} P_2^2 M_{*2} \right)^{1/3}
\]
\[
a_2 \propto (P_2^2 M_{*2})^{1/3}
\]
Thus,
\[
\frac{a_2}{a_1} = \left( \frac{9}{2} \right)^{1/3} = (4.5)^{1/3} \approx 1.65
\]
Planet 1 has a ~1.65 times higher transit probability than Planet 2.
